chapters.title: Chapter One: The Basement
paragraphs: Burgundy had been awake for thirty-one hours.
He could tell by the count blinking in  the corner of his monitor, the timer he set to motivate him. He did this. The number didn't bother him. The shake in his right hand did.

The basement smelled like smoking copper. Three monitors glowed green-on-black in front of him, lines of code scrolling so fast they made the dim room flicker. Cables ran along the floor in bundles thicker than his arm, taped down with whatever he'd had on hand: duct tape, electrical tape, in one place a strip of his own shirt. Against the far wall, beneath a tarp, the prototype waited.
He hadn't looked at it in six hours. That was on purpose. If he looked he'd find something to fix, and he didn't have time to fix anything else. Tomorrow was the day.

The monitor on the left was running a simulation of the drill's torque curve against twelve different ore hardness values, plotted in white-on-green. The monitor in the middle was showing the feedback gain table from the strain gauges, the numbers updating every few seconds as the simulation ran. The monitor on the right was open on a text editor, and in the editor, on the third line from the top of a function he had named GO, there was an off-by-one error he had been looking at for almost an hour without seeing.

He saw it now. He pressed the tab key. He pressed it again. He pressed it a third time and committed the fix and ran the simulation again and watched the torque curve resolve into something less ugly than it had been.
He let out a breath. An eye twitched.

Above him, somewhere, the palace was quiet. The palace was always quiet at this hour. Even the kitchens, which started before dawn, had not yet started. Burgundy could hear the boiler in the next sublevel, a low irregular cough that had been part of the basement's soundtrack for so long that he no longer heard it unless he listened. He listened for a moment. Then he stopped listening and pressed his hands against his eyes and counted to ten.
He had been working on this thing for two years. This project no one understood. That he himself sometimes didn't understand. But he kept working.

Two years. Or, that was the official count. The number he gave himself when he was being honest about the project as a project. The truth was he had been working on something like the prototype since he was eight years old, when he had taken apart the desk clock in the receiving room and put it back together upside down on purpose to see if his father would notice. His father had not noticed for two months. When he had noticed, he had cuffed Burgundy on the side of the head and told him to leave the clock alone. Burgundy had taken it apart again that night and put it back the right way, and his father had never mentioned it again.
He thought, sometimes, about the miners. The people the planet ran on.  Their black faces and dying lungs.  The royals wouldn't have a cent to their name without their grueling work.

He did not know any of them well. He could not have. He was the prince, and the prince did not go into the mines except to stand at the rim during inspections, in the embroidered coat his father made him wear, while the foremen read from their clipboards and the King nodded at whatever they said and the miners below in the pits, black-faced, soaked through, holding their picks at their sides like rifles at parade, looked up at him without expression. He had been to the rim of the South 12 Shaft three times in his life. it was the "worst" mine. It wasn't just a pit, but a deep laberynth of tunnels. Burgundy's grandpa's guys found some special vein of ore down there. Never ending. So they just kept digging down.  it has become imfamous for how deep it went. a tangle of tunnels no single person knew the extent of. the elevators to get down to the deepest parts took 30 minutes one way. or so he heard from his uncle who used to sneak out as a teenager and explore. an act of royal rebellion.

Burgundy only knew the surface of South Twelve but remembered the smell. He remembered the way the work lights along the walls made the air look like it was full of something solid. He remembered one miner, a woman with a black face swinging her pick against a wall and directing the black crumbs that came off that wall into an impossibly old cart. Her sweat seemed permanent.
He thought about her, sometimes. A lot, actually.  in fact the entire thing he was building, a robot with a drill attached,  could trace back to her.  A machine that could replace that woman.

He had not told anyone this. He was aware that it was the sort of thing that would sound stupid if he said it out loud, I built it for a woman whose name I do not know, and he was aware that this was also possibly true.
His father did not know about the basement.

Or, Burgundy hoped his father did not know about the basement. It was possible that he did. The King had a way of knowing things that he never said he knew, and then producing them in court like a magician producing a coin, weeks or months after he had first learned them, when the production would do the maximum harm. Burgundy had watched him do it to advisors. He had watched him do it to ministers. He had never watched him do it to family, but the family was small, just the three of them, and Burgundy had learned to assume his father knew everything until he had proof he didn't.

On Dross you had one child if you were lucky enough to keep one. That was true in the quarters and true in the palace, and Burgundy had grown up inside it the way you grow up inside a weather. A shaft did not care whose son you were. The planet had taught everyone the same arithmetic long before it taught them anything else: raise one, and pour everything into the one, because there was rarely enough of anything to divide.

Still: the basement was his. It had been a wine cellar once, before some great-great-uncle had decided wine was beneath royal dignity. The bottles had been carried up and broken in the courtyard. Burgundy had read about this in one of the old palace ledgers,  He had taken the cellar over when he was twelve. He had run the cables down himself, through a vent shaft he had widened with a drill over a long summer.  Everything else he had scavenged: a loader motor left to rust in the eastern yard, ball bearings from a broken serving cart, copper wire he stripped from a wall no one had lit in years. He carried it down a piece at a time, at night, and no one ever asked where it went.
He had told himself, sometimes, that he was preparing for something.
He had not been sure, until tonight, what.

The tribute ships came every month and he had watched them for as long as he could stand at a window. When he was very small he had asked his father what they loaded into the massive vessels. what were they taking away from our planet and what did we get in return? Everything, his father had said.

He had learned, eventually, the name of the man who wanted it. He had never met the man. Nobody on Dross had ever met the man. Nicholas was a name his father said the way other people talked about the season's rainfall, as a fact of the world. It was all Nicholas.
Burgundy finished wiring up the robot's arm. he toggled his controllers to test it out. fluid and smooth. this was working. it would be impressive tomorrow
He had been careful in his rehearsals not to imagine his father's response.
His mother had given him a glance, at dinner.

That was all. A glance. She had not said anything to him during the meal. She rarely did, when his father was present. But at one point, when the King had been talking to one of his ministers about the southern tariff and Burgundy had been pushing food around his plate without eating it, she had looked at him across the table, briefly, and then looked away.

The table was never only the three of them. His father held court over meals the way he held it over everything else, and the long board ran down into low light, filled most nights with the men who ran the small planet.

That night it was the finance minister, The governor of the northern fields, down from the iron country for the season's accounting, the master of the eastern works, who laughed at the King's jokes half a beat before they finished. Two security men whose names Burgundy had never been offered. Three of the men had brought wives, and the wives wore dresses that had crossed systems to reach Dross, cut from cloth no loom on the planet could have made, this was a sampling of the elite layer of the planet. They spoke endlessly about things and people Burgundy did not know or have any interest in.

The governor's wife asked him once whether he was enjoying the season. He said he was. She smiled and turned back to the others, and that was the whole of his participation. Around him the southern tariff was raised, weighed, and settled in the mild tones men use when the argument has already happened somewhere else. His father spoke last on it, briefly. The minister nodded. The governor nodded.
Burgundy answered when spoken to, and behind his eyes the simulation went on running.

And then his mother shot him that looks again. She was trying to get his attention.  But something was certainly amiss in her mind. He had spent his whole life noticing the things she did not say and trying to assemble them, and he had never quite managed it. Sometimes he thought she watched him the way you watch a clock you have built yourself, waiting to see whether it will keep time. Sometimes he thought she did not watch him at all and he was inventing it.
He was probably inventing it.

The code terminal blipped. The torque simulation had finished and produced an output graph he stared at for almost a minute before he understood what he was looking at. The graph was fine. The graph had been fine the last three times he had run it. He was running the simulation because he could not think of anything else to do, and he could not think of anything else to do because he was very tired.
He looked at his hand. Still shaking
He looked at the timer in the corner of the monitor. The number had ticked over to thirty-two.
He thought, I should sleep.
He thought, I cannot sleep.

He opened the editor again. He scrolled to the bottom of the GO function. He stared at the bottom of the GO function for a while. He moved the cursor up two lines. He moved it down again. He did not type anything.
The boiler coughed below.
Somewhere far above him, the palace clock struck three.
He laid his head down on his arms.

He told himself it was only for a moment. He told himself he just needed his eyes to stop hurting. He told himself a few more things, small reasonable things, and then, between one of those things and the next, he was no longer telling himself anything at all.

The basement was dark and green and full of small mechanical noise, and the code flittered against his face like moths against a screen, and somewhere far above the palace, the planet kept turning toward the day he had spent two years preparing for, the day he had no way of knowing would not go the way he had rehearsed.

chapters.title: Chapter Two: The Court
paragraphs: The receiving hall of the palace was not beautiful. The King had spent his wealth on other things: huge statues, a collection of hunting portraits in a corridor no one used, a fountain in the courtyard that had not worked in years. droves of staff. The hall itself was tall and cold and made of grey stone the color of wet ash. There were no tapestries. There were no banners. At the far end, on a dais three steps high, sat the throne.
His father sat on it.
Burgundy had not planned to arrive late.

He had planned to wake at five, with an hour to wash and rehearse the pitch one more time and walk the prototype up the spiral stair without anyone seeing him. He had not planned to wake at seven, faceprint on his sleeve, the hours-counter showing thirty-five, his neck stiff in a way he could already tell would last all day. He had washed his hands and face in cold water from the basin in the basement. He had changed his shirt. He had pulled the tarp off the prototype and he had wheeled it up the stairs without speaking to it.

In the thin morning light of the basement the robot looked smaller than it did at night. It stood on its one fat wheel, chest-high, the salvaged frame bolted and rewelded until the seams showed like scars, on what looks like a round metal chest and torso with two arms. One for grabbing, and one for drilling rock. The cutting bit at the drill arm's end was ground down to a dull working shine. Low on the front of the robot was a green-glass panel, where his code lives. the brain of the thing positioned where the heart would live, this morning holding a slow green pulse, indicating "active", and Burgundy looked at it whole for the first time in six hours and thought, before he could stop himself, that it was either the best thing he had ever made or a toy, and that in a few hours his father would decide which.
The doors of the receiving hall were never open during the council hour. He had been walking past them his whole life. He had never walked through them carrying anything before.
Today here he was, pushing the great doors open and walked through them.

The prototype rolled at his side on its single fat wheel. The wheel was loud against the stone. Burgundy had not noticed in the basement how loud it was. Down there the cables and the ventilation hum had absorbed the sound; up here in the cold expanse of the hall the wheel sounded like someone dragging a coin across a slate.

Boy and Robot were walking toward the king, who was broad through the chest, his hair going silver at the temples. A serious expression etched permanently into his face. When Burgundy had been very small he had thought his father was the largest thing in the world. He still thought so sometimes in dreams.

His mother stood beside the throne. Mira's hair was dust-grey, and she wore a gown the color of dried blood. She did not smile when she saw her son. Burgundy felt her watching him . He searched her face for the look she had given him at dinner the night before, the brief one, across the table, and he could not find it. She was looking at him a different way now.

Three advisors sat at a table with stacks of papers at the foot of the dais, old men in old robes, the kind of men who had been advisors when Burgundy was born and would be advisors when Burgundy died. They watched without expression.  The one on the right had a smear of ink on his white collar he did not know was there. The one on the left looked at the prototype briefly and then away.
"You asked to see me," the King said.
"Yes, sir."
"This is the council hour."
"I know, sir."
"Then I assume you have something worth the council's time. What is this?" his eye shooting to the robot.

Burgundy stepped forward. The wheel was loud again, the prototype rolling with him into the open space at the foot of the dais and parked itself there as he had taught it to, a small command, hours of code, written for this single moment.
It parked and lit up, the panel on its chest pulsed green. It made a soft sound, almost like clearing its throat.
"Father," he said. "I want to show you something."
That was not what he had planned to say.  But the words came out anyway, and the prototype was already glowing, and there was no taking it back, so he kept going.

"It mines," he said. "Or it will, in the fields. Twice as fast as a man with a pick. Maybe more, with proper tuning. I built it from scrap. The components cost less than a month's pay for a single miner. If we built a hundred —"
"Stop."
The King had not raised his voice. He did not need to.
"Father —"
"I said stop."
Burgundy stopped.

The hall was very quiet. The wheel of the prototype was no longer moving, and so the hall was, for the first time since Burgundy had entered it, fully silent. The advisors were looking at the floor. Mira was looking at Burgundy. The King was looking at the prototype as if it had crawled in on its own.
"What do you imagine you have built?" the King asked.
"A miner. A better one."
"And what do you imagine I will do with it?"
"Whatever you want. You're the King. You could —"
"I am the King. yes" His father said it gently, almost patiently, the way one might explain a familiar fact to a young child. "And do you understand what that means?"
"It means —"
"It means I rule. I rule this planet. But not really, I dont rule this planet.
Then a pause. long than was comfortable.
"Men." he said softly "I rule men. I do not need to mine the mines faster. I need to rule the men who mine them. Do you understand the difference?"
Burgundy did not answer. His throat was too tight.
The King stood.

He was tall, and he came down the three steps slowly, his robe whispering as they brushed against the stone and he stopped in front of the prototype. He looked at it for a long time. He did not touch it.
Then he looked at his son.

"You think I haven't seen this before," he said. "You think you're the first person to bring a clever invention to a throne. There have been a hundred of you. Every one of them believed he had discovered the thing that would change our world. Make our lives better. Do you know what changes the world, Burgundy?"
"What."

The word came out smaller than he had wanted. He knew is father would pepper with rhetorical questions and he had practiced answering what with the right amount of dignity. But here, now, with the wheel silent and the green panel pulsing and his father an arm's length away and Mira's eyes on his back, the word came out the way it had come out of him at eight years old, holding a clock he had taken apart wrong.
"Will," the King said. "Will, and patience, and the willingness to do unpleasant things to keep order and peace."
His voice was almost kind.

"You are my son. You will rule one day. Ruling isn't just ruling. It a craft. Our craft. It is not learned by playing with robots. It is learned at my side. And you have not been at my side. You have been hiding in the dark, playing with wires, while I have been ruling. What I have given you is the future of this kingdom. And you bring me this?"
He kicked the prototype.

It was not a hard kick,  the prototype rocked back on its single fat wheel, and the green panel flickered, and somewhere along the right side of the hall one of the advisors made a small soft sound that might have been a laugh and might have been a cough.
Burgundy heard it.

In the basement, in the long hours of the night, he had run every scenario he could imagine for how this conversation might go. He had imagined the yes. He had imagined the no.  He had been careful, he remembered now being careful, not to imagine a laugh. He had not been able to bring himself to imagine a laugh.
But the laugh had not come from his father.

The laugh, or the cough, he would never know which, had come from an old man with ink on his collar, an old man whose name Burgundy was not sure he had ever known, an old man who had been standing in this room since before Burgundy was born.
"Take it away," the King said.
"Father —"

"Take it away, Burgundy. Do not bring it back. Do not bring me anything like it again. The next time I see you in this hall I want to see you in council robes. Listening. Learning. Not in overalls. Not with grease on your hands. Do you understand me?"
Burgundy looked down at the prototype.
"Yes, sir," he said.
He did not look at Mira.
He did not look at the advisors.

He turned the prototype around, by hand, because he did not trust himself to give it a command in a voice that would not crack, and he pushed it back toward the doors. The wheel with the loud sound again. The hall behind him silent.  Burgundy walked the length of the hall with his hands on the prototype's housing, and at the doors he did not stop, and he did not look back, and he pushed through into the corridor.
The doors closed behind him.
He stood for a moment with his hand on the prototype, in the long cold corridor where his footsteps would have echoed if he had taken any. He stood very still. Shaking to himself
The prototype hummed beside him. Its green panel pulsed once, gently.

chapters.title: chapter 3 Mira's wing
paragraphs: burgundy stood there.  Muffled through the doors of the receiving hall, the council resumed. His father's voice came through as a low rumble without shape. Then one of the advisors was speaking. Then his father again, longer, and something that must have been a joke because it was answered with soft polite laughs.
He was still listening when the small side door in the corridor, a door he had walked past his whole life without registering, opened.
His mother slipped out.

She did not look at him. She closed the door behind her without a sound. She stood for a moment with her hand still on the handle, listening to the council, until the King said something else that was answered by the same polite noise, and then she turned to Burgundy, and she put one finger against her lips.
"Come," she whispered. It was less a word than a breath. "Bring it." her eyes dashing to the robot
Burgundy opened his mouth.
She shook her head, a single small motion, and turned, and began to walk down the corridor.

He put his hand on the prototype's housing. He pressed the small command that told it to follow. The prototype rolled after him. he had built it with a tracking module keyed to his terminal and, since three weeks ago, to a small pin he had begun carrying in his pocket. Where the pin went, the robot followed.
They walked.

They took a corridor Burgundy knew, the long one that led past the council chamber toward the eastern courtyards, for about thirty paces. Then Mira turned right, into a smaller corridor Burgundy had walked twice in his life, and he began to lose his bearings.
She took him past a door he had believed was a broom closet. Behind the door was a narrow flight of stairs going up.
She started up them without hesitation.

Burgundy stopped at the foot of them, looking. The prototype stopped behind him. Its wheel, a single fat wheel, salvaged from a serving cart, rated for stone floors and stone floors only, was going to have to descend stairs.
He had prepared for this, sort of.

Two months ago, in the basement, he had cut the wheel open. He had lined the inner rim with a segmented rubber sleeve, and he had wired a small compressor into the prototype's chest cavity, and he had programmed a soft-mode that would let the sleeve slacken enough for the wheel to deform around the edges of steps. It had worked once, on a test stair he had built out of scrap in the corner of the basement. He had never taken it up or down a full flight. He had not been sure he would ever need to.
He pressed the command.

The prototype's chest made a small hydraulic sound. The wheel visibly relaxed,  it looked, for a moment, as though it had lost some air, and Burgundy pushed it against the first step. The wheel deformed. It caught. He pushed. The prototype rocked forward and down, awkward but functional, and mounted the first step, and then the second, and then a rhythm settled into it that was almost a walk.
Mira was three steps up, watching.
"You built this?" she asked quietly
"Yes."
She nodded once and kept climbing.
The stairs went up two flights. At the top, the walls changed.

Burgundy noticed it before he understood what he was noticing. The stone at the top of the stairs was a different color, warmer, cream instead of grey, and the sconces along the walls were made of a metal he could not immediately identify, worked with a pattern that looked, when he looked closely, like nothing he had seen anywhere else in the palace. The pattern was intricate and repeating. It looked like waves, or like maps. The air smelled different too. Not the wet-stone smell of the palace's lower halls. Something drier and older: books, mostly, and a faint mineral scent underneath that he could not place.
Mira did not stop to let him look.

She took him through a small anteroom and into a larger corridor with a high vaulted ceiling and windows on one side, all shuttered, all dusty. Their shoes made no sound; the floor here was carpeted, a long red runner going grey. Burgundy realized, walking down it, that the runner had not been walked on in months. Possibly years. Possibly he was the first person to walk on it who was not his mother in a very long time.
"Mother, where —"
"Not yet."

They passed doors. Most were closed. One was open a crack, and through it Burgundy caught a glimpse of a sitting room set up for guests who had never come, chairs still angled toward each other in conversation with no one. The whole wing had the feeling of a play that had been rehearsed once and then never performed.
They turned a corner. They turned another.
Mira stopped at a set of double doors, pushed them open, and stepped through.
The library.

Burgundy had known there was a library in the palace. There were several. The one near the entrance, where his father sometimes met with foreign envoys, had a wall of leather-bound treaties and a globe that had not been updated in his lifetime. The one off the council chamber held the ledgers and the tax records and the tribute receipts. Neither of them was this.
This library was three stories tall. bug deep into the basement

The shelves ran floor to ceiling on all four walls. There were ladders on brass rails that traveled the length of each wall. There was a spiral staircase in the center that went up to two levels of galleries. There were tables, long, dark, oiled tables, with reading lamps and stacked books and, on one of them, a small model of a star system Burgundy did not recognize. There was a globe. There were, so far as he could see at a glance, tens of thousands of books, and half of them were not in any language he had been taught to read.
He stopped.
The prototype rolled up beside him and stopped too, its wheel humming back to solid mode, its soft-mode air-cycle finishing with a small sigh.
Mira let him look for a moment. Then he asked, "Mother, what is this place?" She said, without turning:
"This is my library. This whole wing is mine. built at my request when I agreed to marry your father. My mother sent most of these books. this is a piece of my family"
"Your family," Burgundy said.
She turned.

For the first time since the corridor she smiled, a small, thin smile, without warmth, without unkindness either. The smile of someone acknowledging a fact that had been true for a long time before the other person had learned it.
"Yes," she said. "My family."

She crossed to a shelf on the eastern wall, second gallery up. She climbed the ladder without hurrying, and Burgundy followed her up because he did not know what else to do, and the prototype waited below on its wheel, its green panel pulsing slowly in the low light. At the top of the ladder Mira walked along the gallery to a specific shelf and stopped in front of it.
The books on the shelf were mostly grey and brown. A few had gold lettering.
One was yellow.
She reached up and put her hand on the yellow book, a plain yellow, no title on the spine, and she looked at Burgundy.
"This," she said, "was your grandfather's."
Then she pulled.

The book came out an inch, then stopped. Something inside the shelf clicked, a small mechanical sound, quiet but precise, and the whole bookcase shifted on some hidden hinge and began to swing inward, silently, like a great door on very old bearings that had been very carefully maintained.
Behind the bookcase was another room.
Burgundy had built rooms.

He had built the basement, over three years, from an old wine cellar. He had built the workshop in the eastern hills, the one Mira did not yet know about, or so he had assumed, from a sealed vent chamber. He had walked into his own rooms enough times to know what a workshop looked like when the person who used it had made it themselves, from what they had, in the dark.
This was not that.
The room behind the bookcase was white.

Actually gleaming white. The walls were paneled in some smooth pale material that was not stone and not wood and not metal exactly, but held light the way a page holds ink. Overhead, no torches, no oil lamps, no hanging bulbs, ⟪a row of long flat panels shed a clean cold light Burgundy had only seen once before in his life, in the receiving hangar where the tribute ships parked.∷a row of long flat panels shed a clean cold light Burgundy had seen only in the technical workshops, where the royal engineers bent over their long drafting tables, in the years when his mother still took him along to watch.⟫
Along three of the four walls ran long white work tables.

The tables were clean. They were laid out with equipment. Not scrap. Not salvage. Real equipment: sealed processors in their original packaging, still bearing manufacturer's marks.; oscilloscopes newer than anything the palace had bought in his lifetime; a small array of green-glass panels stacked between wooden dividers; toolboxes with drawers labeled in a fine hand he recognized, after a moment, as his mother's.

Against the back wall stood a low shelf of documents: folders, ledgers, thin bound reports, all with the same neat spine tags. A stack of manifests. A stack of star charts. A stack of what looked, from where Burgundy stood, like schematics.
He did not step into the room.
Mira did. She walked to the nearest table and set her hand on it lightly, as though checking that it was still there.
"Come in," she said. "Bring it."
Burgundy stepped in.

He walked to the first table. He picked up a processor. He turned it over. It was a model he had read about in a manual six years old and had never, in the manual or in life, expected to see in his own hand. It was worth, at black market prices, more than a year of a miner's pay. There were twelve of them on this table alone.
He set it back down. His hand was shaking again, though not from tiredness this time.
"Mother," he said.
"Yes."
"What is this room."

Mira crossed to a chair near one of the tables and sat down. She sat the way she sat at council, straight-backed, hands folded, but her face was different than it was at council. She looked, for the first time Burgundy could remember, like a person and not like a queen.
"Your father does not know about this room," she said. "That is the first thing to understand."
"All right."
"Nobody in your father's line has ever known about this room. The Queen's wing was built with certain conditions attached. My family attached them. This is one of them."
"Your family?" Burgundy said again, because he still did not understand what she meant when she said it.
She looked at him.
"Sit down," she said.
He sat.
"You know that I was not from here," she said. "You know that your father married for the alliance. That is the version that is told at court. It is not exactly a lie. But It leaves things out."
"What does it leave out."
She considered the question. She considered it the way she considered questions from advisors: a full pause, the small tilt of the head, the calculation of what to give and what to keep.

"My family," she said, "is not a family in the way your father's family is. There is no title. There is no throne. There is no country. There is only a network. The network is very old and very large and it is spread across nine systems that I know of and possibly more. It moves things. Some of those things are legal in some places. Most of them are not legal anywhere. What we move most of, and what has kept us in business for the last two centuries, is minerals. Specifically the sort of minerals that are used to build the sort of processors you are holding."
Burgundy looked down at his hand. He had picked the processor up again without meaning to.

"Dross is not important to the empire. But Dross is very important to us. to my family. We move a great deal of what Dross produces. Not through the tribute channels, those are Nicholas's, and my family and Nicholas have an understanding, but through the other channels. The channels that do not appear on your father's ledgers.
She paused.

"Dross has been secretly trading with our people for years," she said, "they've always been able to find enough minerals in this planet to not only pay the tribute but also to sell to the shadow market.  But it was always full of mistrust. My people aren't just traders. they're pirates. they raid and steal and when your father's father wanted to formalize trade ties, my family offered a solution. The solution was a marriage, an alliance built on trade and trust. The marriage was me."
Burgundy could not think of anything to say.
"I was seventeen," Mira said

"I didn't have much of a choice, I was young, and even though I had dreams of my own I was the family bargaining chip, every generation has one. I knew I had to be sent here to this place. So I asked for the library. I asked for a whole wing to be built so I could continue my studies. My family agreed to fund it. Your father's family agreed to build it.

For for the last 19 year I've been buying from the far away systems, using my family's smuggling routes. Every cargo vessel that comes to collect Dross minerals carries a second, hidden manifest, the things I've requested. My cousin runs the family's Dross trade. She has been very helpful."
Burgundy tried to hold all of it at once and could not.

His mother was a pirate. Not the daughter of some distant royal house, the way he had always been told. Her family was a cartel, raiders and smugglers who moved black-market cargo across nine systems. Though in a way, he thought, that made her royalty after all. Any family that controlled that much trade would command more wealth than most thrones.
And here she sat, surrounded by parts and machines and parts Burgundy hadn't known existed. All of it smuggled onto the planet under her husband's nose.
Burgundy had spent two years believing the basement was the one big secret in the house. But there had been two secrets, and his was the smaller one.
"How does Father not know about any of this?"

"He believes that what I do here is read books and give instructions to servants who no longer exist. He has not been in this wing since our marriage. He has never opened the door to this library. He is not curious."
She said the last word — curious — with something like tenderness. It was the first tender thing Burgundy had heard her say all morning.
"Why?" said Burgundy, looking at his mother as if for the first time.
"Why what?"
"Why buy all of this?"

"Because I am curious. I always have been, about the world, about the way gadgets and inventoins like this can feel like magic. My grandfather lived through the coming of interstellar travel, and when I was a girl he would tell me how it changed everything. Whole systems pulled out of poverty in a generation, because suddenly they could trade with empires across the stars."
There was a pause. Then Mira said:

"So I have been collecting. And more than collecting. A disc slipped into a servant's basket now and then, carried down to the quarters where someone might read it. A better pump sent to a village that had been hauling water by hand. Small things, quietly, for years." She looked at him. "The people of this planet believe they are poor because the universe made them poor. They do not know they have been cut off from it on purpose."
Burgundy did not know how to answer.
"I decided a month ago that I was going to show you this room. Because I've been watching you in the basement"
"you know about the basement?"
"I have known about the basement for more than a year, Burgundy. I've said nothing because I wanted to see how far you would take it on your own."
Burgundy said nothing.
"You brought it to him today" She continued, "your robot. I knew you would. And I guessed the outcome. I told myself that if your father rejects it, it would be time to show you this."
They stood in silence. She walked to one of the tables. and picked up a spool of fine-gauge wire and turned it over in her fingers, once, and set it back down where it had been.
"I am going to offer you a bargain," she said. "Listen carefully. I am going to offer it once."
"All right."

"This room is yours. Everything in it. The parts, the tech. the tools.  Whatever else you need, tell me, and I will get it from anywhere in the system. Even from the core worlds I can get a fair number of parts.  You will not have to smuggle scrap out of the southern shaft anymore.  You will build here, in this room, with real materials. I have collected discs with some of the most up to date research. and you will build whatever you want to build."
She looked at him.
"In exchange," she said, "you will be the prince your father wants."
He looked at her.

"You will show up to council every morning, You will wear the coat. You will listen.  You will visit the mines with your father when he goes, and you will nod when he speaks, and you will smile the way he wants you to smile. You will be seen at the tribute inspections. You will attend the seasonal meeting with regional governors.  You will travel to the docks each month with him to see the tribute shipment goes smoothly. You will be, in every public detail, the son he wanted to have. If he calls on you to speak, you will speak, and you will say what he wants to hear. "
"He'll never believe it," Burgundy said.

"He will," Mira said. "He will believe it because he wants to. That is the thing about your father you have not yet understood. He does not see what is in front of him. He sees what he expects. Give him what he expects, and he will not look further. He will believe that the lecture he gave you after he shut down your prototype created a change of heart and that you've grown up, just like he always knew you would."
Burgundy sat with his hands in his lap. He did not look at the processors on the table. He looked at his mother.
"You are asking me to become him," he said.

"I am asking you to look like him. just to keep his eyes away from what you are doing here. if he finds out about this room and my support of you, it will end very poorly for all of us. Do we have a bargain?"
He thought about it.

He thought about his father kicking the prototype. He thought about the small sound the advisor with ink on his collar had made, the sound that might have been a laugh. He thought about the woman in the South 12 Shaft who had not looked up at him. He thought about the tribute ships coming down each month.
He thought about his father saying I rule men.
"Yes," he said. "We have a bargain."

They stood in silence, Burgundy's mind racing as he saw his mother, or some version of his mother, for the first time. And so much started to make sense. the stories she would tell about inventors and gadgets that connected the stars, the errands she would take him to visit the royal engineer. How he would find tools and gadgets on his shelf. in his toy bin. he realized that this moment wasn't random. This was by design. This was his mother's design.
She crossed the room and picked up something from the far table, a small object he could not see clearly until she brought it to him, and she pressed it into his hand.

It was a tiny processor unit. Not the one he had picked up first. A shinier, newer looking one with fine gold lines worked across its surface in a pattern he could not read, close and deliberate, the kind of work no tool on Dross could have cut.
"Begin," she said. and left.

chapters.title: chapter 4 double life
paragraphs: From that morning on, Burgundy's life was never the same.

He began living two lives. Throwing himself into the work of being the perfect prince, and throwing himself even harder into the work he did when no one was watching. The first life happened in daylight, in halls, in coats. The second happened in a white room behind a yellow book and mostly atnight. For eight months, neither life knew about the other, and Burgundy carried both with increasing fear that his father was on to him.

but the more time passed  the more he realized mira was right. His father seemed to believe nothing was amiss. that he believed the lecture had worked. the King saw the son he expected to see, the boy finally bent into shape, and he did not look further. Burgundy watched his father not look further, morning after morning, and filed it away.
He listened.
That was the thing about council that surprised him: how much there was to actually learn, once he stopped resenting the room.
He learned the tribute.

He had known about Nicholas his whole life but more like a child knows a fairytale. Now he learned the mechanics. The arrangement was old, older than his father, older than his grandfather. Nicholas provided security. That was the word the ministers used, security, always without irony, and it took Burgundy three months of listening to understand everything the word contained. Dross sat in a remote system, months of hard travel from the core lanes of the Alliance. The Alliance's markets were real but distant; its protection was theoretical. A planet full of minerals with no fleet of its own was more of a warehouse with the doors unlocked. Nicholas kept the doors locked. Nicholas's ships patrolled the approaches, and Nicholas's name, more than his ships, kept the raiders of six systems from descending on Dross. In exchange, Nicholas took the ore. Most of it. The royalty of Dross had resented the bargain for four generations and complied with it for four generations, because it worked, and because nothing else would. Every resource-rich planet in the region lived under some version of the same arrangement. It was not an alliance. It was extortion with a schedule. The ministers did not call it that. Burgundy learned not to call it that either, out loud.
He learned the mines.

Not the rim-of-the-shaft version he had been shown as a child,  the real accounting. Dross harvested eleven commercially significant minerals. Iron in bulk from the northern fields, where the seams ran shallow and wide. Copper and tin from the eastern hills. And from the deep shafts in the south,  the dangerous ones, the ones that took lives,  the specialty ores, the ones that were worth shipping across systems: dense blue-black corvite, which was refined offworld into the substrate of every processor in the whole galaxy; threnite, which held a charge; pale veins of osmarine, which the ministers priced per gram. He learned that a single crate of refined corvite was worth more than a year of the northern fields' iron harvest. He learned that the corvite in one of the processors on his mother's white tables had, in all likelihood, come out of the ground less than forty kilometers from where he sat, shipped offworld raw, refined in some distant system's foundries, assembled into components, sold to fuel the alliances advance computer systems but also onto the shadow market, smuggled back in by his mother's cousin, and set on a table sixty meters above the shaft it had been cut from, at a markup of roughly ten thousand percent.

Nobody on Dross could build a processor. That was the arrangement. That was the whole arrangement, seen from the right angle. Dross sold the flour and bought the bread, and this explained, finally, why his father was so aggressively averse to any kind of technological development on the planet.  why his "craft" was ruling men to mine year in and year out.
He learned the army.

He had grown up thinking of the palace guard as the army. It was not. The army was three thousand men in barracks near the major shaft complexes, and it had not fought an external enemy in living memory, because external enemies were Nicholas's department. The army existed for domestic disputes. That was the ledger term: domestic disputes. It meant strikes. It meant slowdowns. It meant the year before Burgundy was born, when the southern shaft workers had refused to go down for eleven days and the army had gone into the workers' quarter and afterward the ledgers showed a one-time expense labeled pacification and repair. The army existed to keep the miners mining. Burgundy sat in council and watched his father review the army's budget with the same attention he gave the tribute, and understood that his father considered them the same expense.
He learned the festivals.

This was the lesson that stayed with him longest. Twice a year, at New Year's and at the midsummer Descent, the King opened the storehouses. Alcohol for every workers' quarter, paid from the royal accounts. Three days of suspended shifts. Music, lanterns, the great drum lines that Burgundy had heard from the palace walls his whole childhood, a low thunder rolling up from the city that he had always assumed was simply what joy sounded like.

The midsummer Descent, his tutors had told him, went back to the Ghai, the mining people who had ruled Dross before his father's line, who marked the longest day by descending together into the oldest shaft to hang lantterns for their dead, to sing and drum and chant a cathardic chant and refusing to bring up a single stone, then followed by two days of feasting and lamp-lit processions, and folk music and spirit worship. Their marriages would happen during this festival.

And under the King’s alcohol the Descent had an older fuel: something the elders drank from shallow cups that glowed faintly in the dark, a smell like hot metal and rain on road, passed hand to hand in the oldest rites.

Millions of people lived on Dross in conditions that anyone looking honestly would describe as slow grinding attrition, and twice a year the cities below the palace erupted into celebration so bright and loud it could be seen from orbit, and Burgundy had grown up believing this proved something about the spirit of the place.
It did prove something. He just had the something wrong.

He was at his father's side, eight months in, reviewing the festival provision, the King signing off on the alcohol allotments line by line, generous, unhurried, when his father said, without looking up:
"Do you know why I pay for this?"
"No, sir."

"Because a man who has something to look forward to does not burn down what he has." His father signed the last line. "Remember that. It is cheaper than the army, and it works better. Men do not rebel in the weeks before a festival. They do not rebel in the weeks after, while they are still telling stories about it. Time it right and you are never more than a few weeks from safety." He set down the pen. "That is the craft. Nobody will teach it to you honestly but me."
Burgundy nodded the way he had learned to nod.

Some days, that was the hardest part of the whole performance, not the pretending, but the learning. His father was a careful ruler. That was the thing Burgundy had not expected. The cruelty was not stupidity; it was, as his father always said "craft", refined over generations, applied with patience. The festivals, the army, the tribute, the shaved stipends. It all fit together, it all worked, and his father moved through it with the fluency of a man who had genuinely mastered his inheritance. Burgundy sat at his left hand and nodded and learned the craft of ruling men, and told himself he was learning it as reconnaissance, and was never fully sure this was true.
The nights belonged to the white room.

He found his own ways up. That was the first project. His mother's route through the broom-closet stair was hers; using it risked pattern, and pattern risked notice. So Burgundy went up instead of down. The palace's roots were deeper than its towers old dungeon galleries, drainage vaults, dead corridors sealed and forgotten by men who had died before his grandfather was born, and the Queen's wing, he discovered, had been built onto a disused arm of that complex, its foundations grafted into the old cells. Over the first month he mapped three separate routes from the basement to his mother's wing, each surfacing through a different forgotten door. He took a different route each night. He never told Mira which ones. She never asked.
In the white room, for the first few months, he read.
The knowledge came on discs. And the discs, he came to understand, were the shape of the whole civilization.

There was no living connection between the stars. That was the fact underneath everything, the fact the Alliance's own maps politely minimized: information could be beamed between worlds, but a signal was months crossing what a ship crossed in weeks, decayed and stuttering by arrival. So knowledge moved the way freight moved: in batches, on hulls. The great relay stations of the core worlds gathered transmissions the way harbors gather cargo, wrote them onto discs, and the discs rode out along the trade lanes toward the periphery. A disc was a slab of pressed crystal the size of Burgundy's palm, dense with more text than the palace's three libraries combined, and by the time one reached Dross the research on it was a year old at minimum, often three. It did not matter. On Dross, three years behind the core was still fifty years ahead of anything else on the planet.

Mira's cousin brought the discs in with the cargo runs. Burgundy would slip his mother a written list, never spoken, always written, folded into the book she was reading at breakfast, and two or three months later a crate would arrive in the white room with the discs pressed between wool packing, labeled in a language he had begun teaching himself. Journals of the core-world academies. Engineering proceedings. Foundry specifications. And, the ones he read until the text swam, the code research.

The core worlds had a discipline for it. That was the revelation that reorganized his entire understanding of what he had been doing alone in a basement: whole academies, generations of researchers, devoted to the study of programs that were not simply programs, but rather livingthings. Code that had the ability to teach it self to be better. Or was least that was the theory. From his reading it was clear that no one in the core worlds had been able to implement this idea into anything useful. It was still locked up in the minds and and labortories of academies and theoreticians.  He read papers on feedback architectures. He read papers on selection pressure applied to instruction sets, on programs bred like livestock across ten thousand generations in a single night, on the strange and apparently unresolved arguments about how far the technique could be pushed before the program's own goals drifted out from under its maker. Half the mathematics was beyond him. but with time he taught  himself, disc by disc, working backward through citations, filling notebooks and becoming more aware than ever that he had a mind that closed on hard things and did not let go. It wasn't easy, but it wasn't hard either.  He was seventeen and he was receiving, in batches, stale and secondhand, the advanced education of a core-world engineer.

chapters.title: chapter 5 Mira's Shipment
paragraphs: One night in the ninth month the white room had to wait.

Mira came to his door after the palace had gone quiet. She did not knock in a way that could be heard from anywhere but the door itself. When he opened it she was already turning to go, and she said only, "Wear something dark. Not the coat."
He did not ask.

They went down, not up. She took a route he did not know, out a gate in the north wall that a guard opened without looking at either of them, then along a track running east, toward low ground beyond the cargo field where the tribute loaded. Burgundy had assumed ships came down on Dross in exactly one place. He had been wrong about most things his mother touched.

There was a second field. Smaller. Lit only by shielded amber lamps set low along its edges. A freighter sat on it with its running lights dark, not one of Nicholas's grey giants, which never landed at all, but a working hull, scuffed, patched, a third the size, resting on struts. Its cargo ramp was down.
Nobody hurried. That was the first thing he noticed. The loaders rolled crates up the ramp on low sleds, hydraulics sighing under the weight, steered by men who had done this a hundred times.

A woman met them at the foot of the ramp with a slate under her arm. Was this Ressa, his mother's cousin? He quickly learned this woman spoke for Ressa. Burgundy had imagined the cousin did these deliveries herself.

She held the slate out to Mira. "Manifest's ready. Ressa signed the outbound this afternoon.  The medicine order is short two pallets. The vendor's problem, not ours." Then, with a glance at Burgundy that lasted no more than a half a second then back to Mira, "is this..."
"yes" Mira said cooly
The woman snuck one more glance at burgundy then turned back up the ramp signalling to the loaders to proceed.
Burgundy watched.

Up the ramp went the crates of ore. He knew it by the stenciling now: density codes, grade marks, black corvite in sealed bundles. And beside the ore, in a separate stack the crews handled differently, more slowly, in padded cradles: casks. Small. Banded with metal. When a loader tilted one to seat it on the sled, the seam of the lid showed a faint glow, cold and steady, like a coal that had decided to stop burning and only remembered how to shine.

He knew what it was. He had heard the word over the years. Mostly in a whisper: Kiln. A drug of some sort.  The substance that fueled the spiritual dimension of the midsummer Descent. Refined from a rare seam-mineral in a method the Ghai had discovered. fleks of it consumed with the root of a stone weed and used as sacred in the old rites; illegal in every system that bought it anyway because it was a stimulant that ran a man for two days and gave him blissful visions. This was Dross's second harvest, their cash crop, made of rock.

Down the ramp came the arriving cargo. Seed stock in heavy sacks. Casks of oil. crates marked in other languages. And, at the end, a stack of boxes of the kind Burgundy recognized. Machine parts stamped in three languages, small wool packed wooded boxes full of discs from the core world.

It was worrisome to have it all out in the open like this. The crew carrying his secret down the ramp on dollys like any other shipment. But to them this was just another crate. It may look suspicious to his father, but His father didn't ever come to these shipments. Hadn't for years. He preferred Mira to be the interface.
Mira looked at one of the crew and said "Lew." and nodded her head at the bundle of items.
Lew must have been the insider that Mira paid to get all this from the cargo field to the white room behind the bookshelf.
Lew gave almost no acknowledgment that he had heard but went straight to gather the boxes and crates onto a motorized loader, and off he went into the dark.

Mira was finishing now. She initialed a line on the clipboard. She stopped at another. "This count is wrong. there were only 17 casks." The woman on the ramp checked; it was. Mira corrected it herself, small precise figures, the same hand that labeled the toolbox drawers in the white room. here it was running Dross's second economy.

chapters.title: chapter 6 DREKKO
paragraphs: The nights turned from studying discs to actually building. The hardware changed everything. The processors from Mira's tables ran his feedback code four hundred times faster than the salvaged board in his first prototype; simulations that had taken a night now took a minute, which meant he could be wrong four hundred times as often. The crates brought hydraulics of a kind Dross's own industry had never seen,  sealed actuators, compact and vicious, that could put three tons of pressure through a joint the size of his fist. They brought strain sensors finer than anything in the mines, servo assemblies, spun-carbon frame stock that weighed a third of the salvaged loader steel.

this made building easy by comparison. like putting together a puzzle. and By the end of the first year there were three prototypes of his drilling robot. he would call this generation 2 of a robot he was now calling "DREKKO".

They stood in a row along the white room's western wall, and they no longer looked like the machine his father had kicked. The single serving-cart wheel was gone; each unit now ran on a pair of independently driven treaded tracks that could soften or stiffen on command, his old sleeve-and-compressor trick, rebuilt with real components, so that the machines climbed the dungeon stairs behind him with a rocking, patient  easy gait. Each carried twin drill arms on hydraulic mounts, a cutting head he had ground himself from offworld tool-stock, a sorting bucket slung between the tracks. In their chests, behind green glass, the  advanced processors ran his code. He had rebuilt the feedback architecture three times from what the discs taught him. The machines scored their own work now, depth of cut, energy spent per kilogram, waste ratio.
They were, by any measure that had existed on Dross a year ago, marvels.

he would test the robots' ability to mine on a practice wall he found in the deepest room of his dungeon routes, an old cell gallery whose back wall, he had discovered in the second month. It was not built basic stone but of valuable mineral: the palace's foundations sat directly on the shoulder of the southern ore country, and somewhere in the centuries , when power shifted hand, the new ruler had built the palace atop an old mine. there was still unmined riches here. Burgundy had tested the rock out of habit, and the sensor mast had come back with a reading he made it repeat three times.
Corvite. A seam of it, thick at the room, running diagonally through the rock like a vein of night.

It was, he understood, a small fortune sitting inside the palace's own foundations, unmined because unmapped, unmapped because no one had ever thought to mine the dungeons. It was also, more usefully, the perfect teacher. Corvite was the hardest ore on Dross: dense, brittle in the wrong ways, prone to shattering into worthless gravel if the cutting angle was wrong by even a few degrees. The southern shafts lost more men to corvite seams than to any other work. If the machines could learn corvite, they could mine anything on the planet.

So every night, after council, after the coat came off, Burgundy went down through the old galleries and set the three prototypes against the wall, and watched them try. He moved his array of computers form teh white room to this dungeon-turned testing room so he could work down there and watch the robots try to cut into the rock

They were not failing, exactly. That was what made it hard. Each unit could bore into the seam. Each could strip freed ore into its bucket, sort waste rock by density, back out, and resume. Watching them work, a foreman from the southern shafts would have wept. three machines, no lungs to ruin, no stipends, no festivals required, chewing steadily into the hardest ore on the planet.

But The pace was wrong. He clocked them against the numbers he now knew from council: a good southern crew, twelve miners with picks and a blast allotment, pulled roughly a ton of raw corvite in a shift, losing a third of it to shatter. His three machines together managed perhaps half that, losing a quarter. Better per machine than a man. Not better enough. At this rate, replacing one shaft's crews would take three hundred machines, and he could build, with every disc and every crate and every stolen midnight hour, perhaps one every 90 days.

And they did not improve the way he needed them to.  they did not do whathe discs said they could with the right mix of code and hardware. and That was the true wall. His feedback code let each machine tune itself, a better angle here, a smarter torque curve there, but the tuning flattened out. Each prototype would improve for a week, ten days, and then settle onto a plateau, grinding away at the seam with a competence that never became mastery. He would adjust the scoring, and the machine would climb a little, and plateau again. and He  once again was the bottleneck. Every real improvement still ran through him: his diagnosis, his rewrite, his upload. Three machines waiting on one exhausted seventeen-year-old's judgment, and the seventeen-year-old was spending his days nodding at tribute ledgers.
18 months. Three machines, and a plateau he could not code his way past.

Some nights he sat on the cold floor of the gallery with his back against the old cell bars, the notebooks piled beside him, the green panels pulsing their patient rhythm against the dark, and did the arithmetic again, all the theoritical math the smartest minds in the galaxy had published promising code and hardware that would learn and grow like a human brain.  It never did. What he had built was remarkable. What he had built was insufficient. The distance between those two facts was where he lived now,  and he had begun to suspect, in the grey hours when the drum of the drills blurred into the sound of his own pulse, that no amount of his own cleverness would close the gap. He could not think fast enough to set these three machines free to think for themselves.

chapters.title: chapter 7 The Bridge
paragraphs: It began on a spring morning, 20 months after his mother first swung open the bookcase, and it began the way every important thing in Burgundy's life had begun: disguised as an ordinary day.

The day was worse than ordinary  in fact. It was mundane in the specific, grinding way that palace days could be mundane: a morning council about grain storage, a midday audience with a delegation of northern foremen whose grievance took two hours to state and one sentence to deny, an afternoon review of festival provisioning that his father conducted line by line, signature by signature, while the light moved slowly across the council chamber floor. Burgundy sat through all of it. He nodded in the right places. He had been nodding in the right places for almost 2 years now, and the nodding had become so automatic that he sometimes caught himself doing it alone, at night, at his workbench, agreeing with no one.
The whole day, one thought sat behind his eyes like a coal.
The discs.

His mother had passed him a new crate the week before, and this batch was different. He had known it was different by the third page of the first disc, read standing up, coat still on. For years the research he devoured had lived on one side of a canyon: software that could improve itself, code breeding code, selection pressure applied to instruction sets in clean simulated worlds. On the other side of the canyon stood his machines, real hardware, real rock, real dust clogging real joints.  A program could remake itself a thousand times a second, but it was still reasoning about a body it could not feel, in a world it could not touch, and so every real improvement still had to cross the canyon on Burgundy's back.
The new discs were about the bridge.

Core-world teams in top labs, three of them, working the same problem from different directions, their papers arriving on Dross pressed together on one crystal wafer, had begun closing the loop through the hardware itself.  producing experiments in a lab that showed real promise. The machine's own sensors feeding the machine's own learning, every strain gauge and thermal reading and torque curve pouring into the scoring functions in real time, like human senses to a human brain. The papers called it "closed-loop embodiment algorithms."

ANd the night before this spring day, Burgunday had read them all, three times each. and that's when it hit him The papers were brilliant but they were blind. Each team had proved the loop could close, in simulation, on a rig, in a world scrubbed clean of the things that made his machines choke, the real world. dust, heat, physics. and none of them, he saw, reading the same three authors argue past one another, had ever spent a night on their backs under a machine with sealant on their hands. They were so deeply confident in their controlled worlds that they missed that the hard, filthy, unglamorous work of making it survive contact with an actual world was beneath the math, or beyond it, or simply invisible to men who had never held a tool. And Burgundy, reading in a stolen room, on a backwater planet, with grease under his nails and years of failure, understood something that surprised him: He knew things they did not. He saw solutions that they could only argue about with vague words and concepts like "real world industrial application scenarios". He was...ahead of them.
He got back to the white room that evening before the lamps in the workers' quarter came on, and he worked.

he arrived with a new clarity on his problem, potentially the final frontier to making the robot teach itself:  the sensor buses on his prototypes had been built, by him, in a different life, to report their readings on a fixed cycle to a fixed log. The learning loop needed them raw and constant, a firehose instead of a faucet, a waterfall of real time data.  But every time he opened the data channels all the way, the processors drowned. The scoring functions fell behind the sensations they were supposed to score. The machines got clumsy, worse than before, drunk on their own feeling, and twice that night a drill arm slammed a cutting head into the corvite at an angle that sent shatter pinging off the gallery walls like shrapnel.
he had to replace a drill arm, twice that night something he had done 20 times by now.

He tried throttling the flow. He tried batching it. He tried letting the machine choose its own sampling rate, which the second paper hinted at and the third paper warned against, and the warning proved correct in a way that cost him a hydraulic line and an hour on his back under the second prototype with a mix of sealant and lubracant on his hands.

By the fourth hour of the night he had stopped being methodical. He knew he had stopped and he let it happen. There was a mode he went into, past a certain hour, that he did not entirely trust and could not entirely do without, where the experiments stopped being designed and started being thrown. He rewired the sensor buses on all three machines in three different configurations. He wrote four scoring variants and could no longer remember, by the end, which machine carried which. He gave them access  to the micro-charge dispensers he had mounted on their arms a month earlier, these were little explosives the size of beads, dispesed from magazines within the robots' arms. He had never used thembefore, they were meant for an experiment in pre-fracturing the rock, but he had shelved the idea as too dangerous to automate.  but tonight he was letting everything fly. He set bounds on the charges. He checked the bounds twice to make sure he wasn't about to blow up the whole foundation of the castle.

Then he lined the three prototypes up against the seam, barely scarred by two years of their patient, insufficient chewing, and he loaded the whole reckless suite of experiments into the queue, every variant, every configuration, set to run in rotation, each machine scoring itself and passing what it learned sideways to the other two.
He looked up, and the high thin slit window of the cell had was ilumnating with a warm sharp light.
Dawn. He had done it again. Council was in two hours and he had not slept in, he counted, twenty-six hours. He had to press go on this flurry of code and machinery and leave.
Wash, coat, council, foremen, docks. The tribute came down today.
He looked at the three machines idling against the black seam, their green panels pulsing, the experiment queue loaded and waiting on his word.
"Go," he said tio himself and pressed one button on his keyboard and left them working, as he often did.

He did not look back at the wall. If he had, there would have been nothing to see. It looked like every other morning he had left them: three patient machines, a barely wounded vein, a boy going up the old stairs two at a time with his coat over his arm.
Council was a blur

He got through the grain reports. He got through a dispute between two southern governors . Twice his head dipped, the full nod, chin to chest, and the second time he came back from it to find the room silent and his father looking at him down the length of the table.
"Am I boring you," the King said.
"No, sir. I apologize. I was reading late."
"Reading."
"The northern field reports." The lie arrived without being sent for. A year and a half of practice.
His father studied him a moment longer. "Read earlier," he said, and turned back to the table, and Burgundy exhaled through his nose, slowly, the way you let pressure out of a line.

The main business of the council was "groups." which was the royalty euphemism for gatherings of disgruntled citizens who were discussing strike or rebellion or anything of the sort.    There had been "groups" in the workers' quarters. Secret ones, at night, in the drying sheds and the pump rooms, the third such network broken up in a year. The word strike had been used; the interior minister said the word committee, which Burgundy had learned in almost two years of council was the word this room feared most. Six men had been taken. The minister recommended, and the King approved, that the taking be kept quiet, because with the festival five weeks out, quiet plus festival would bleed the pressure better than any public lesson.

"They are tired," the King said, signing. "Tired men make threats in sheds. Then the drums start and the drink is poured, and they remember they have something to lose, and they lose interest in losing it." he chuckled to himself. He set down the pen and looked, briefly, at his son, a teaching look, checking that the lesson had landed. Burgundy nodded

But something in his chest had leaned forward, listening, because there was something new in what the minister had said: six men taken, a third network in a year, the pressure rising faster than festivals could bleed it. And Burgundy filed the numbers away with all the other numbers, down in the dark where he kept them.

The tribute came down at midday, and Burgundy stood on the observation platform at his father's right hand and watched, as he had watched every month for almost two years, and it had never once stopped being the most alien thing he had ever seen.

⟦From the platform, while they waited, the whole planet lay open around him. The sky was the pale hard white it always was, a sky the color of nothing, never fully blue and never fully dark, and under it the city climbed toward the palace in terraces of grey stone and rust roofing, hills of it stacked on hills, until the last feeble strip of forest gave out and the land opened into the pit country, the great open wounds of the southern shafts. He had watched all of this from a window his whole childhood. Now he could price it per gram.⟧

Nicholas's ships did not land. That was the first thing about them, the thing that reorganized your understanding of what a ship was. They arrived out of the white sky, three of them today, each the length of the palace and its grounds laid end to end, and they stopped, and hung, a hundred meters above the cargo field, without wings, without scaffolding, without any visible negotiation with gravity. Their hulls were the grey of deep water and utterly unmarked, and they made a sound that was less a sound than a pressure, a low field of force that Burgundy felt in his molars and in the bones of his chest, and that made the whole field of stacked crates, ten thousand tonnes of ore, graded, weighed, sealed, a month of the planet's blood in boxes, look like an offering laid out of fear. which is what it was.
Then the arms came down.

They unfolded from the bellies of the ships in silence, joint after joint after joint, white and precise, each one long enough to reach from the palace gate to the throne, and they began to pick up the crates. thirty-tonne crates rising in gentle clusters, drawn up into holds that never showed their insides. Nicolas's soldiers  stood on the field in their painted safety rings and watched, hard men with hooks on their belts.

⟦The platform behind them held the usual small court of the field: two regional governors in grey formal coats, the tribute master with his ledger men, a colonel of the domestic army standing where he could watch both the loading and the crowd that watched it. They stood at his father's shoulder with the ease of men who had stood there their whole lives. The ore was Dross's. The field, Burgundy understood without being told, belonged to them.⟧
Burgundy was so tired that the membrane between his two lives had gone thin, and the day-prince stood on the platform in his coat while the night-builder counted joints, estimated torque
He could not help it.

If those arms had a feedback loop, he thought, they would teach themselves to sort mid-air, to nest the ascending clusters tighter, to shave a second off every lift and then a second off the shaving. The thought belonged to the night. And behind it, because he was too tired to keep the two rooms separate, sat the machines he had left against the seam that morning, and the small bright hope that the explsoive had not brought the castle down on them.
His head dipped.

He caught it, half a second, no more, and came back to the pressure-hum and the white sky, and found his father looking at him. Not with anger. That was the strange thing. The King had seen the dip, and something in his face was almost soft.
"You're tired," the King said, quietly, under the hum.
"Yes, sir."
His father turned back to the field, to the last crates rising into the grey hulls, and he was silent for a while, and then he said, still watching the ships:

"You've become a great prince. I want you to know I see it. You'll be king someday, sooner than either of us would like, the way the years are going, and for the first time I believe you're ready for it. More than ready." He paused. The arms folded themselves away, joint after joint, into the bellies of the massive ships. "I'm glad you gave up those childish things. The toys, the wires. I know it wasn't easy, it never is, giving up what we love first. But look at you." He nodded at the field, at the order of it, at the month's blood rising into the sky on schedule. "This suits you. This is right for you. This is what you are."
The ships went up without seeming to move, the way the sun crosses a sky, and were gone, and the pressure lifted out of Burgundy's molars, and the field was just a field again, emptied.
"Thank you, Father," Burgundy said.
It was, he reflected, walking off the platform at his father's side, the kindest thing his father had ever said to him.

He was released from his duties an hour before dusk. by the time he reached the last of his three routes through the old galleries he was running, coat over his arm, taking the worn stairs down in the dark by memory.
He smelled it before he saw it.

Rock dust. In the hallway. thick. Not the ordinary haze the prototypes raised in a night's work, a thickness in the air of the hall of the old jail cells, a mineral fog that hung in the light of his lamp, and under it a smell he knew from exactly one place in his life: the rim of a working shaft. Blasting residue. Deep rock, opened.
He came around the last turn into the his cell-turned-lab and stopped.
The wall was gone.

Not damaged. Not advanced upon. Gone — where the seam had been, where almost two years of patient insufficient chewing had left a scarred black face, there was now a hole. A tunnel. Round-shouldered, clean-walled, taller than he was, driven straight into the living rock, and so deep that his lamp simply failed inside it, the light falling into the dark the way a stone falls into a well.
The three prototypes were not in the gallery.

Burgundy stood at the mouth of the tunnel for a long moment, listening to his own pulse beating on  hisneck, and then he did the thing that almost two years of discipline had built into him: he went to the terminal first.
The logs were still streaming.

He read standing up, then sitting, then leaning into the screen with both hands on the desk, scrolling, not breathing right. The queue of reckless experiments had run in rotation, as designed, for the first two hours after he had left, variant after variant failing in the old familiar ways, drowned processors, drunk actuators, one logged shatter-event that had cost the second prototype a cutting edge. And then, in the third hour, one configuration on the third machine, one of the ones he had wired past midnight and could barely remember, had caught.

Caught was the only word for it. He watched it in the logs the way you watch a spark take in dry grass. The data firehose and the scoring loop had synchronized — not throttled, not batched, but phased, the machine sampling its own body in rhythm with its own actions, feeling each cut as it made the cut, and the performance line, flat for almost two years, had bent upward. Then the third machine had passed the configuration sideways to the other two, as designed, and all three lines had bent, and then the loop had begun doing the thing the papers promised could happen but never achieved, and Burgundy had never once seen with his own eyes:
It improved the improving.

Every second, the logs said, each machine was taking in its thousands of tiny sensations, torque flutter, thermal bloom, the acoustic signature of rock about to shatter versus rock about to yield, and converting them into micro-adjustments: a cutting angle shaved by a tenth of a degree, a charge from the micro-dispensers placed not where the rock was weakest but where the next three cuts would want it weakened, the blast so small and so exact that it did the work of an hour's grinding in a sound no louder than a knuckle crack. And each adjustment fed the next. And the rate of adjustment was itself adjusting. The curve in the logs was not a line bending. it was a line turning into TKTKTK
He looked at the numbers at the bottom of the stream, tonnage, waste ratio, energy per kilogram, and he did not believe them, and he checked them against the sensor sums, and he believed them.
Then he took his lamp and went into the tunnel.

The tunnel was beautiful. That was the thing he had not expected, and it undid him a little, walking through it. The walls were not rough-bored but finished, cut in long smooth strokes that overlapped like the grain of planed wood, and at intervals along the floor, in neat staged rows, sat the ore. Processed. The machines had not just cut the corvite free; they had pulverized the waste rock and packed it into the voids behind them, and the corvite itself they had crushed, graded, and pressed into dense dark bundles the size of bread loaves, wrapped in sheeting from their own supply spools and stacked with a regularity that no human crew on Dross had ever achieved or attempted. He picked one up. It was heavier than it looked. It was worth, at the ledger prices he now knew by heart, more than a southern miner earned in half a year, and there were dozens of them, staged at intervals.

He walked on. The tunnel dipped, and turned, following the vein. He could see where the machines had made choices, where the seam had forked and the cutting pattern showed a moment of exploratory nibbling before committing,  and he had gone perhaps three hundred meters, far beyond any map of the palace foundations, when the character of the walls changed, and he stopped.
The machine-cut smoothness ended at an edge as clean as a doorway. Beyond it, the tunnel was still a tunnel, but an old one.
